topic: Blog share: what does recovering from burnout actually look like?
text:
People recovering from burnout often say they are better, but not well. That gap is common, and it is worth naming in the consult.

Long-term research from Swedish stress clinics found most people treated for burnout improved a great deal, though only some described themselves as fully recovered years later. Lower tolerance for stress was the most common thing that lingered, along with tiredness, sleep and concentration difficulties.

People also described recovery as a long road with setbacks, in which what helped changed over time: quiet, low-effort rest early on, then shorter and more active recovery later. Acceptance and adjusting their lives helped many of them.

In our new blog, Natalia Cajide looks at what this means day to day, from rest and switching off to memory, focus and the return to work.

Read the blog: https://equalpsychology.com.au/blog/recovering-from-burnout-what-recovery-looks-like

Key sources:
Glise, K., Wiegner, L., & Jonsdottir, I. H. (2020). Long-term follow-up of residual symptoms in patients treated for stress-related exhaustion. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-020-0395-8
Aronsson, I., Stigsdotter Neely, A., Boraxbekk, C.-J., Eskilsson, T., & Gavelin, H. M. (2024). Exploring the process of long-term recovery in people previously diagnosed with exhaustion disorder. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-024-01756-z
